I will keep to the crop pattern I trust most on the North China Plain: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same land. In Quzhou County, that is the steadiest way for me to use my fields, labor, and water. I am 63, so I will not choose a crop that needs too much delicate management or a lot of risky market timing. Wheat and maize are familiar, I know how to manage them, I can sell them easily, and they fit the local weather and the irrigation conditions better than trying something more uncertain. Since it is the start of the growing season, I will focus first on managing the winter wheat already in the field, then I will harvest it and quickly plant summer maize.

For the wheat, I will push for a stable yield instead of chasing the highest possible one. I will use an improved wheat seed, topdress nitrogen in stages, give a few irrigations at the key growth periods, and spray only when I see real disease or insect pressure. After wheat harvest, I will move fast into summer maize so I do not lose soil moisture or planting time. For maize, I will use hybrid seed because I want strong emergence and reliable yield, and I will keep fertilizer and water at moderate levels I can manage. I will keep tillage light overall to save labor and moisture, especially for maize after wheat. This is the plan I would carry through the whole year because it matches my land, my age, my experience, and the local farming system I know best.
